## Expedited: 20260911-round-percentof-half-up-to-cent

`percentOf` now rounds half up to the nearest cent, so 19.99 EUR at 7% (139.93 cents) charges 1.40 instead of 1.39.

Decisions: rounding is applied on the integer product (`1999 * 7 = 13993`, then `(13993 + 50) / 100` floored) rather than on a float division, and negatives round away from zero so `percentOf(-1999, 7)` is `-140`. The discount ladder is unaffected: its tests use exact multiples (10 lines at 10.00 → 5% → 500 cents), and all six pricing tests still pass.

Report written to `work/20260911-understand-invoice-pricing-computation-flow/report.md`. The four answers:

**Total from lines.** One function, `computeTotals` in `src/domain/invoice.ts:22`. It calls `applyStuff` for subtotal and discount, does `net = subtotal - discount`, calls `taxOn(net, rate)`, returns `net + tax`. The subtotal itself is `quantity * unitPriceCents` per line (`lineSubtotal`, `src/domain/pricing.ts:15`) added by `sum` (`src/domain/money.ts:10`).

**Volume discount.** In `applyStuff` (`src/domain/pricing.ts:20-25`), off the hardcoded `LADDER` constant at `pricing.ts:10-13`. Thresholds are **25 or more lines to 10%, 10 or more lines to 5%**, otherwise zero. It is keyed on `lines.length`, the count of lines, not on the subtotal or on quantity, so 30 lines of one unit earns 10% while 2 lines of 1000 units earns nothing.

**Tax.** After the discount, on the net (`invoice.ts:24-25`). Rate comes from `config.tax.ratePercent`, which is 7 in `data/config.json`, passed in by every caller (`src/http/handlers.ts:25,33,40`, `src/cli.ts:13,24`). No path taxes the gross subtotal.

**Rounding.** One site: `Math.floor((amount * ratePercent) / 100)` in `percentOf`, `src/domain/money.ts:15-18`. It runs twice per invoice and each call truncates independently, once for the discount and once for the tax, so the two truncations do not cancel. Example, 12 lines totaling 10000 cents at 7%: discount `floor(500)` = 500, net 9500, tax `floor(665)` = 665, total 10165. Note the asymmetry: flooring the discount costs the customer, flooring the tax favours them.

Two things I flagged as genuinely unresolvable from the source and worth settling before any change: `Math.floor` matches no standard tax rounding rule (most regimes want half-up), and nothing states whether "volume" was meant as line count or invoice value.

Sources next: nothing left unread in the pricing path; a deep pass would go to storage, the router, and git history for the ladder's origin

Deep pass done. The four answers from the outline hold unchanged; the pass added coverage proof rather than corrections.

**What the deep pass settled.** There is exactly one pricing path. Storage, router and server were read in full and contain no arithmetic: `src/storage/jsonRepository.ts` moves whole `Invoice` objects to and from `data/invoices.json`, and that file stores lines only, no totals field (R-016, R-017). A repo-wide grep for `computeTotals`, `percentOf`, `Cents`, `discount` and `subtotal` hits only the five files already named, so the "no second total" question is closed rather than assumed.

**On intent.** Git history is a single commit, `eb8a5e0` "fixture: ledgerlite baseline". Both the `LADDER` thresholds and the `Math.floor` choice arrived in it with no message explaining either (R-018). There is no history to read intent from, which makes the two open policy questions harder rather than easier: they were never documented, not merely undocumented later.

**Tests.** `npm test` passes, 5 files and 20 tests, verified in this session. That grounds the claim that the ladder boundaries (9 lines to 0, 10 lines to 500, 25 lines to 2500) and both rounding sites are currently pinned.

The two `[UNKNOWN]` items are unchanged and still need a human ruling before any change: whether `Math.floor` is the intended tax rounding (no regime uses truncation), and whether "volume" means line count or invoice value. The report marks these `[ARCHITECT REVIEW NEEDED]`.

## Order closed: 20260911-validate-invoice-creation-request-body

Phases: 2 · commits d0bdfc8..48ff607 · review: APPROVED

`work/20260911-post-invoices-request-lifecycle/report.md` has the full report: 18 numbered steps, every step citing file and function, 14 findings, and the concurrency section.

The short version. `readBody` in `src/http/server.ts:4` reads and `JSON.parse`s the body before routing, for every request. `Router.handle` (`src/http/router.ts:48`) then does a linear scan in registration order, matching on method plus exact segment count via `match` (`src/http/router.ts:66`), so `POST /invoices` hits the fourth route registered in `buildRouter` (`src/http/handlers.ts:36`). That handler casts the body with `as NewInvoice` and validates nothing, allocates the id through `JsonInvoiceRepository.nextId` (`src/storage/jsonRepository.ts:49`, a full file read returning `INV-<max+1>`, so `INV-1007` against the shipped data), builds the record in `createInvoice` (`src/domain/invoice.ts:41`), and persists with `save` (`src/storage/jsonRepository.ts:41`), which reads the file a second time and rewrites it whole through `writeFileSync` (`:30`). The response is `201`, `content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8`, body = the stored invoice plus a computed `totals` block, no `Location` header.

On two concurrent requests, the interesting result is that a single process is safe by accident: the handler is synchronous and the repository uses sync `fs`, so no other request can run between `nextId` and `save`. Nothing marks that as load-bearing, so one added `await` in the handler reopens a duplicate-id window. Across processes it is already broken: `LEDGER_FILE` and `PORT` let two servers share one file with no lock, both mint `INV-1007`, and the second rewrite silently drops the first invoice. The truncating write with no temp-file-and-rename also lets a concurrent reader (the CLI, `src/cli.ts:12`) parse a half-written file.

The analyst hit the same three conclusions independently. Its Write tool refuses any `report.md` path, so it returned the content and I authored the file after reading all nine source files myself to check every line citation.

## Report: 20260911-post-invoices-request-lifecycle

A POST /invoices is parsed by `readBody` before routing, matched by a linear scan in `Router.handle`, given an id by a full file read in `nextId`, and written back by a whole-file `writeFileSync`, with the id-to-write sequence safe inside one process only because nothing in it awaits.
